newsitem.title: UK: Emerging Europe Advertising & Media Digest -Aug 19.
newsitem.headline: Emerging Europe Advertising & Media Digest -Aug 19.

text.p: REUTERS EMERGING EUROPE PRESS DIGEST FOR ADVERTISING & MEDIA
Weekly Press Digest from Central and Eastern Europe on Advertising,
Marketing, the Media, the Internet, Brand-name Products and Consumer Trends.
ADVERTISING & MARKETING:

-- The Czech Republic's A-Z advertising agency wins advertising contract for IPB Real, a real estate development company. A-Z will create two ad campaigns for new housing estates in Prague's Troja and Vinice districts. (Strategie
News, July 6-13, 1997)

-- Television advertising sales in the Czech Republic in the first half of 1997 topped 3.0 million crowns ($87,600), about 500,000 crowns above year-earlier levels, A-Connect advertising reports. Print advertising sales rose 18 percent to about 3 million crowns in the 1997 first half, while radio advertising sales reached 158,329 crowns. (Pravo, August 15, 1997)

-- Unilever remained the Czech Republic's largest advertiser in the 1997 first-half, spending 190.4 million crowns. Procter & Gamble retained its number two spot, spending about 164 million crowns. Henkel CR was ranked third, spending 127 million crowns. Henkel was the ninth largest advertiser in 1996. (Strategie News, July 6-13, 1997)

-- The Peoplemeter, a tool for measuring television audiences, has yet to find widespread favour in the Czech Republic. "Advertising agencies have not yet shown much interest in the results of Peoplemeters," says Vladimir Jurecka, marketing manager for TV Nova. He expects it will take 10 years for Peoplemeters to be the main criteria in placing television advertising.
(Strategie News, July 6-13, 1997)
MEDIA & THE INTERNET:
-- Metro, Prague's new daily newspaper available free in metro stations,
meets with unexpected interest in its first week of publication, says
Editor-in-chief Jiri Vavra. Strategie News says sales of daily newspapers in
newsstands near metro stations have fallen 10 to 30 percent since Metro's
introduction.(Strategie News, July 6-13, 1997)
-- Hungarian consumers can order more than 100 different furniture products
of RS Butoraruhaz via the Internet. Goods are delivered within three days,
with customers paying cash on delivery. The firm hopes that within three
years 80 percent of its sales will be made on the Internet. (Vilaggazdasag,
August 12, 1997)
-- Hungarian telecommunications firm Westel 900 GSM Rt sets up its new centre
in Debrecen at a cost of 600 million forints ($3 million). Westel has
invested 80 billion forints in its Hungarian network and the number of
subscribers has increased from 200,000 to 330,000 over the past 10 months.
(Vilaggazdasag, August 13, 1997)
BRAND-NAME PRODUCTS & CONSUMER TRENDS:
-- Poland's Seat car dealers report selling more than 10,000 vehicles in the
first six months of 1997, with highest sales registered for the Cordoba and
Ibiza passenger car models. (Dziennik Prawa i Gospodarki, August 12, 1997)

-- Hungarian retailers continue to sell consumer goods with forged trademarks at fairs and markets, according to Hungarian consumer protection watchdog FVF. The most frequently forged trademarks include Nike, Fila, Kappa and Budmil. (Vilaggazdasag, August 11, 1997)

-- The three-day Hungarian Formula 1 Grand Prix race attracted a record 205,000 spectators and ticket sales totalled 1.2 billion forints. Of total visitors 70 percent were foreigners, including 48,000 from Germany.
(Vilaggazdasag, August 14, 1997)

-- Poland's CPC Amino food company claims a 45-percent share in the country's concentrated soup market. It claims a 70 percent share in the concentrated sauce market and a 23 percent share in mayonnaise products. CPC Amino's licenced brand name products include Knorr, Hellmans, and Alsa.
(Rzeczpospolita, August 13, 1997)

-- The quality of perishable foods offered by Poland's shops and restaurants is declining, with 29 percent of outlets selling products past their expiry date, the state trading standards' authority (PIH) says. (Dziennik Prawa i
Gospodarki, August 8, 1997)

-- Although one in six Hungarians say they try to eat healthy foods, 40 percent eat what they like, regardless of health, according to a survey by GfK-Hungaria market research institute. One in every 10 Hungarians eat out regularly, while half never go to a restaurant. (Vilaggazdasag, August 14,
